title: Study Abroad Report
paragraphs: From March to April 2024, for two months, I was allowed to study at the Medical University of Vienna in Austria. Including the preparation period, it was about two years from when I first started thinking about studying abroad, and I think through this program I learned a great deal and had a wonderful experience that I will never forget.

Neurology at the University of Vienna is divided into three floors: stroke, neurodegenerative diseases and movement disorders. On the first day of my clerkship, a student who likes Japan spoke to me, and I was assigned to the movement disorders group. In Vienna, final-year students do their clerkships while receiving a salary and play a role like that of Japanese residents. They communicate confidently with patients, take histories and do physical examinations, and report to the senior doctors, and although it was as I had heard, I strongly felt the difference in experience. Also, at the lunchtime lectures there were many questions, such as about the specific dosage and selection of drugs, aimed at being actively involved in medical care oneself, and I felt the difference. I too examined patients every day together with the students, but because it was in German I could not read the charts or take histories, so I ended up training to differentiate diseases relying only on physical findings, and unintentionally I think I gained the ability to elicit and think about findings. Also, by going a little early in the morning and being allowed to do ward blood sampling and placing IV lines in the outpatient clinic, my procedures also improved considerably.

In thoracic surgery, Dr. 中西 and Dr. 佐伯, Japanese fellows, looked after me greatly, and I was able to learn the differences in surgery from Japan. There were many cases of advanced lung cancer of a kind not seen in Japan, and I felt there may be a problem that preventive medicine such as health checkups is not sufficiently widespread. Also, lung transplants were performed about once every three days. In Vienna, because the donor's declaration of intent is by an opt-out system, there are said to be many organ donations. I was fortunate to be allowed to see an organ retrieval from a donor, and when we rushed by private jet to a hospital about 45 minutes from Vienna, a heart team and a gastrointestinal team from Germany had come, and about 20 people in total were involved. When everyone was assembled, a midline incision was made in the chest and abdomen and the organs were carefully removed. The sight of the hearts and lungs that had been beating filling with perfusate, turning white and stopping was very impressive, and when we returned to the university and the lung we had retrieved was given to the recipient, I was truly moved. I was also allowed to see the pre- and post-operative outpatient clinics and saw the lung transplant recipients living healthily, and I could realise the wonder of transplantation. Donation after cardiac death was also under discussion, and it became an opportunity to think deeply about the ethical issues surrounding organ transplantation. Being able to talk about our own countries' healthcare systems with fellows who had gathered from around the world, such as Italy, Spain, Portugal and Turkey, is also a good memory.

I am interested in family medicine, and one of my goals was to learn about primary care systems abroad, so, separately from the clerkship at the Medical University of Vienna, through the kindness of Dr. 吉田 I was allowed to visit local private practitioners and met four doctors. One doctor spent an hour on each patient, listening to each disease such as hypertension and osteoporosis and giving care down to the fine details, and another saw 100 patients a day in a poor area with many immigrants, sorting them to specialists as needed and playing the role of keeping patients connected to where they could receive medical services if anything happened. Every doctor saw patients while valuing their own role, and through meeting various doctors I think the kind of doctor I want to become has come into view. When I accompanied a home visit in a country town I was given homemade wine, and I could also taste the fun of being a family doctor who can have deep contact with patients. Also, at the end of the clerkship, in order to observe GPs, I was allowed to do a two-day clerkship at a clinic called Cross Deep Surgery in London. A General Practitioner is a primary care specialist who handles a wide range of patients from infants to the elderly and a wide variety of diseases, and about half of each year's medical school graduates go on to become GPs. In the UK, all residents are registered with a family GP, and when ill they see the GP and are referred to a specialist as needed. A clinic in the UK has several doctors, nurses, social workers and so on, and is like a hospital of relatively larger scale than a typical Japanese one. I had heard that the GP plays the role of a gatekeeper who sorts diseases to specialists, but in fact they handled truly every area, including gynecological care involving hormone therapy, psychiatric illnesses such as depression, dermatological diseases such as rashes and orthopedic diseases, even to quite specialised care, which was very impressive. I have heard that in Japan it is hard to go to obstetrics and gynecology or psychiatry, but in the UK a single doctor treats you, so I felt that it is of great benefit to patients.

In Vienna, regular working hours were 9 to 14 (although I had the impression that in reality they worked until around 16). In exchange, they worked without even taking lunch, and it was very impressive that they were so conscious of being on and off. I was told that they can take one month of vacation a year, and some doctors said they were going to Japan on their next holiday. UK GPs also seem in some cases to take half a year of leave after working ten years, and a doctor who was nearly burned out, partly because of COVID, said that taking leave let them face patients sincerely again, so I think there was a firm recognition that "resting" benefits both oneself and those around. Another thing that was impressive was the male-to-female ratio. In Vienna, even in surgery about half are women, and it was impressive that everyone chooses the department they want to do regardless of gender. One reason is that systems such as maternity leave are well established. They can take nearly half a year off, and I was told they are not driven out of their positions for taking maternity leave. In this way, from the viewpoint of work-life balance I had the impression that it was much better than Japan, but whether there is no strain from that at all, there were also problems, such as not being able to deliver the necessary medical care to patients quickly, for example a one-year wait for hip arthroplasty surgery because of a shortage of doctors, and I also learned that there is no perfect system.

After the clerkship I went to cafes, went to see operas and orchestras, cycled along the river, and traveled to various countries on weekends, having new experiences every day, and the two months really passed in a flash. In particular, attending a ball for cancer charity in formal dress with friends and waltzing until 1 a.m. became an unforgettable memory.

Through various connections, I met many doctors active abroad, such as doctors who had worked for the WHO and Médecins Sans Frontières and Japanese doctors working as GPs in the UK, and could learn various ways of thinking, which was truly valuable for thinking about what kind of doctor I want to become. I was helped by a truly large number of people and could have a fulfilling study abroad: Dr. 吉田, Dr. 清水, Dr. 澤, Dr. Costoner and Dr. Clare, who supported me locally; Dr. 上田 and Dr. 高見, who gave me consultations in Japan and advice during the study abroad; everyone in the International Exchange Office, beginning with Dr. 粕谷; Dr. 長谷川, who supported me with great care; Dr. イッツェル, who always cheered me on strongly and warmly; the seniors in the program; my fellow students who experienced various things together locally; and my family, who support what I want to do at any time. I would like to express my gratitude here.
